Original heading

The distribution of the people.

The people settle in Jerusalem

In every age, people have often preferred their personal comfort and advantage to the common good.

Even those who profess faith frequently seek their own interests rather than the interests of Christ.

Few have loved holy things and places enough to give up their comforts for them.

Yet our souls should delight to live where faithful people and opportunities for spiritual growth are plentiful.

If we have no love for the city of our God, or for anything that helps us enjoy fellowship with the Savior, how will we gladly depart this life to be with the Lord?

To a worldly-minded person, the perfect holiness of the New Jerusalem would be even more difficult to bear than the holiness of God's church on earth.

Let us seek first God's favor and glory.

Let us learn patience, contentment and usefulness in whatever place he has assigned us, looking forward with cheerful hope to entering the holy city of God.
classic_reading:
[Neh.11.1]
Chapter 11
The distribution of the people.
--In all ages, men have preferred their own ease and advantage to the public good. Even the professors of religion too commonly seek their own, and not the things of Christ. Few have had such attachment to holy things and holy places, as to renounce pleasure for their sake. Yet surely, our souls should delight to dwell where holy persons and opportunities of spiritual improvement most abound. If we have not this love to the city of our God, and to every thing that assists our communion with the Saviour, how shall we be willing to depart hence; to be absent from the body, that we may be present with the Lord? To the carnal-minded, the perfect holiness of the New Jerusalem would be still harder to bear than the holiness of God's church on earth. Let us seek first the favour of God, and his glory; let us study to be patient, contented, and useful in our several stations, and wait, with cheerful hope, for admission into the holy city of God.

The priests and Levites who returned (verses 1–26)

We owe faithful ministers a debt of gratitude.

Remember the leaders who taught us God's word.

It is good to learn what our godly predecessors were like, so that we can learn what we ought to become.

The wall is dedicated (verses 27–43)

All our towns and houses should bear the mark “Holy to the Lord.”

A believer should undertake no task without dedicating it to him.

When our hands are to be used in God's work, we should cleanse those hands and purify our hearts.

Those called to help others become holy must first consecrate themselves to God.

For people sanctified to him, the good gifts and comforts of creation also become holy in their use.

The people rejoiced greatly.

Everyone who benefits from a public blessing should share in public thanksgiving.

Temple officers are appointed (verses 44–47)

A day of thanksgiving truly benefits both ministers and people when it leaves them more careful and joyful in fulfilling their duties.

Whatever we do must be cleansed by the atoning blood and through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Otherwise our work cannot be acceptable to God.

The dedication of the wall. | (27-43) |
The officers of the temple settled. | (44-47) |
Verses 1-26
It is a debt we owe to faithful ministers, to remember our guides, who have spoken to us the word of God. It is good to know what our godly predecessors were, that we may learn what we should be.
[Neh.12.27-Neh.12.43]
Verses 27-43
All our cities, all our houses, must have holiness to the Lord written upon them. The believer should undertake nothing which he does not dedicate to the Lord. We are concerned to cleanse our hands, and purify our hearts, when any work for God is to pass through them. Those that would be employed to sanctify others, must sanctify themselves, and set themselves apart for God. To those who are sanctified, all their creature-comforts and enjoyments are made holy. The people greatly rejoiced. All that share in public mercies, ought to join in public thanksgivings.
[Neh.12.44-Neh.12.47]
Verses 44-47
When the solemnities of a thanksgiving day leave such impressions on ministers and people, that both are more careful and cheerful in doing their duty, they are indeed acceptable to the Lord, and turn to good account. And whatever we do, must be purified by the blood of sprinkling, and by the grace of the Holy Spirit, or it cannot be acceptable to God.

Nehemiah removes unlawful influences (verses 1–9)

Israel was a people set apart and was not to mix indiscriminately with the surrounding nations.

Notice the benefit of the public reading of God's word.

When we listen properly, Scripture shows us sin and duty, right and wrong, and where we have wandered from the Lord.

We profit when it moves us to separate ourselves from evil.

Anyone seeking to drive sin out of the heart—the living temple of God—must also remove what supplies it with pleasure and strength.

Take away the food and fuel of sinful desire. This is what it means to put sin to death.

Once repentance has driven sin from the heart, Christ's blood must be applied by faith, and the heart should be furnished with the graces of the Holy Spirit for every good work.

Nehemiah corrects the support of worship (verses 10–14)

Sacred office does not excuse someone from correction or deserved discipline when that person sets an evil example.

The Levites had been wronged because their allotted support had not been paid.

They had gone elsewhere to earn a living for themselves and their families. Their service in the sanctuary could no longer sustain them.

Inadequate support leads to an impoverished ministry.

The work was neglected because the workers had been neglected.

Nehemiah held the rulers accountable.

Ministers and people who abandon religious duties, as well as rulers who fail to uphold them according to their responsibility, must answer for their actions.

Nehemiah acted promptly to restore the Levites to their places and ensure that they were paid fairly.

He continually looked to God and entrusted all his concerns to him.

It pleased him to have been useful in restoring and supporting religion among his people.

He asked God to remember the work, not from pride, but as a humble appeal regarding the honesty of his intentions.

He prayed, “Remember me”, not “Give me what I have earned.”

He asked that his work not be forgotten, not that it be advertised for praise.

Yet God both rewarded him and preserved the record of what he had done.

God does more than we can ask.

Nehemiah stops Sabbath-breaking (verses 15–22)

People seeking to promote godliness must pay attention to keeping the Lord's day holy.

True religion cannot flourish while Sabbaths are treated with contempt.

No wonder Judah's faith and conduct had deteriorated when the people neglected worship and profaned the Sabbath.

Those who profane it often fail to recognize the harm they do.

We must answer for sins encouraged in others by our own example.

Nehemiah condemned their conduct as evil because it sprang from contempt for God and disregard for their souls.

He reminded them that violating the Sabbath was among the sins that had brought earlier judgments.

Repeating the same sins would expose them to further judgment.

His courage, zeal and prudent action provide an example. Henry considers it likely the reform endured.

Nehemiah nevertheless confessed himself a sinner who could demand nothing from God on the basis of justice.

He asked the Lord for mercy.

Nehemiah confronts unlawful marriages (verses 23–31)

If one parent is ungodly, human sinful nature may incline children to follow that parent's example.

This is a serious reason why Christians should not enter marriages that bind them unequally to unbelievers.

Parents must also give careful attention to how their children speak, so that they do not learn the corrupt and irreverent language associated here with Ashdod.

Nehemiah exposed the evil of these marriages.

Those who remained stubborn were punished. Henry explains the physical punishment as ordered through the lawful officers under the civil law then in effect (Deuteronomy 25:2–3), rather than describing a private beating.

He prayed that God would remember them—that the Lord would convince and convert them and remind them of their duty.

Even the best public service may be forgotten by its beneficiaries.

Nehemiah therefore entrusted his reward to God.

His final request also expresses what we most need:

“Remember me, my God, for good.”

We may hope humbly that God will remember us and the service we have rendered, while still acknowledging our sins and seeking mercy after a whole life of useful work.

Like Nehemiah, we have reason to repent deeply and pray to be spared according to the abundance of God's mercy.

Verses 1-9
Israel was a peculiar people, and not to mingle with the nations. See the benefit of publicly reading the word of God; when it is duly attended to, it discovers to us sin and duty, good and evil, and shows wherein we have erred. We profit, when we are thus wrought upon to separate from evil. Those that would drive sin out of their hearts, the living temples, must throw out its household stuff, and all the provision made for it; and take away all the things that are the food and fuel of lust; this is really to mortify it. When sin is cast out of the heart by repentance, let the blood of Christ be applied to it by faith, then let it be furnished with the graces of God's Spirit, for every good work.
[Neh.13.10-Neh.13.14]
Verses 10-14
If a sacred character will not keep men from setting an evil example, it must not shelter any one from deserved blame and punishment. The Levites had been wronged; their portions had not been given them. They were gone to get livelihoods for themselves and their families, for their profession would not maintain them. A maintenance not sufficient, makes a poor ministry. The work is neglected, because the workmen are. Nehemiah laid the fault upon the rulers. Both ministers and people, who forsake religion and the services of it, and magistrates, who do not what they can to keep them to it, will have much to answer for. He delayed not to bring the Levites to their places again, and that just payment should be made. Nehemiah on every occasion looked up to God, and committed himself and all his affairs to Him. It pleased him to think that he had been of use to revive and support religion in his country. He here refers to God, not in pride, but with a humble appeal concerning his honest intention in what he had done. He prays, "Remember me;" not, Reward me. "Wipe not out my good deeds;" not, Publish them, or record them. Yet he was rewarded, and his good deeds recorded. God does more than we are able to ask.
[Neh.13.15-Neh.13.22]
Verses 15-22
The keeping holy the Lord's day forms an important object for their attention who would promote true godliness. Religion never prospers while sabbaths are trodden under foot. No wonder there was a general decay of religion, and corruption of manners among the Jews, when they forsook the sanctuary and profaned the sabbath. Those little consider what an evil they do, who profane the sabbath. We must answer for the sins others are led to commit by our example. Nehemiah charges it on them as an evil thing, for so it is, proceeding from contempt of God and our own souls. He shows that sabbath-breaking was one of the sins for which God had brought judgments upon them; and if they did not take warning, but returned to the same sins again, they had to expect further judgments. The courage, zeal, and prudence of Nehemiah in this matter, are recorded for us to do likewise; and we have reason to think, that the cure he wrought was lasting. He felt and confessed himself a sinner, who could demand nothing from God as justice, when he thus cried unto him for mercy.
[Neh.13.23-Neh.13.31]
Verses 23-31
If either parent be ungodly, corrupt nature will incline the children to take after that one; which is a strong reason why Christians should not be unequally yoked. In the education of children, great care should be taken about the government of their tongues; that they learn not the language of Ashdod, no impious or impure talk, no corrupt communication. Nehemiah showed the evil of these marriages. Some, more obstinate than the rest, he smote, that is, ordered them to be beaten by the officers according to the law, [Deut.25.2] De 25:2, [Deut.25.3] 3. Here are Nehemiah's prayers on this occasion He prays, "Remember them, O my God." Lord, convince and convert them; put them in mind of what they should be and do. The best services to the public have been forgotten by those for whom they were done, therefore Nehemiah refers himself to God, to recompense him. This may well be the summary of our petitions; we need no more to make us happy than this; Remember me, O my God, for good. We may humbly hope that the Lord will remember us and our services, although, after lives of unwearied activity and usefulness, we shall still see cause to abhor ourselves and repent in dust and ashes, and to cry out with Nehemiah, Spare me, O my God, according to the greatness of they mercy.
